rows.case: Devillaz v. Atmosphere Gastropub, Inc. et al
Devillaz v. Atmosphere Gastropub, Inc. et al
Devillaz v. Atmosphere Gastropub, Inc. et al
rows.rationale: Specific tip-pool percentages, an identified manager receiving tips, and an alleged $8.80 hourly wage plausibly support tip-retention and Colorado minimum-wage claims. Missing employment dates, thin individual-employer allegations, and generalized break allegations create partial-dismissal risks, but likely not complete dismissal. Second Circuit overtime pleading rules do not control this Colorado action.

rows.case: Seguin v. Royal Highness, LLC et al
Seguin v. Royal Highness, LLC et al
Seguin v. Royal Highness, LLC et al
rows.rationale: The FLSA tip-retention claim plausibly alleges a specific mandatory pool distributing budtenders’ tips to managers and supervisors, with employment dates, pay rate, duties, and distribution mechanics. Paying above minimum wage does not defeat this prohibition. Managerial-status and commerce allegations have some gaps, and unjust enrichment is vulnerable, but complete dismissal is unlikely.

rows.case: Kluender, Michelle v. Oak Grove Assisted Care LLC
Kluender, Michelle v. Oak Grove Assisted Care LLC
Kluender, Michelle v. Oak Grove Assisted Care LLC
rows.rationale: The complaint plausibly links unpaid overtime and Wisconsin wages to employer-controlled, non-neutral timeclock rounding. Seventh Circuit pleading standards favor survival without exact weekly calculations. Missing examples, unspecified rounding increments, and contradictory employment dates create vulnerabilities, but likely do not defeat every claim. Class certification and rounding neutrality ordinarily require factual development.

rows.case: Rivera v. CHSPSC, LLC
Rivera v. CHSPSC, LLC
Rivera v. CHSPSC, LLC
rows.rationale: The complaint plausibly links recurring overtime to unpaid, interrupted meal periods and excluded shift differentials, with employment dates, duties, shift lengths, and employer control alleged. Missing example workweeks and conclusory willfulness create vulnerabilities, especially because employment ended over two years before filing. Nevertheless, the New Mexico overtime claim provides an independent survival path; certification disputes need not defeat individual claims.

rows.case: McCarthy v. Medicus Healthcare Solutions, LLC
McCarthy v. Medicus Healthcare Solutions, LLC
McCarthy v. Medicus Healthcare Solutions, LLC
rows.rationale: A recurring 50-plus-hour schedule, unpaid overtime policy, and detailed routine duties plausibly support an FLSA claim under First Circuit pleading standards. Exemption likely requires factual development. The principal vulnerability is limitations: employment ended outside the two-year window, making survival depend on adequately pleaded willfulness. Alleged knowledge and selective overtime payments support, but do not establish, willfulness.

rows.case: Timberg v. Toombs et al
rows.rationale: The recurring 10 a.m.–8 p.m. weekday schedule and alleged nonpayment plausibly satisfy Second Circuit overtime pleading requirements despite missing pay rates. Dated wage arrears and quantified loans and expenses independently support wage and contract claims. Exempt status is not established by the managing-director title alone. Weak spread-of-hours and collective allegations may narrow, but likely will not eliminate, the case.

rows.case: Mizzero v. Albany Med Health System
Mizzero v. Albany Med Health System
Mizzero v. Albany Med Health System
rows.rationale: Alleged five-day, ten-hour schedules, an identified overtime week, quantified unpaid pre/post-shift work, and employer instructions plausibly satisfy Second Circuit overtime pleading standards. FLSA and NYLL claims likely survive even if meal-break, rounding, or class allegations are narrowed. Missing pay rates and template errors are unlikely to defeat all claims.

rows.case: Latipov et al v. AN Enterprise Inc et al
Latipov et al v. AN Enterprise Inc et al
Latipov et al v. AN Enterprise Inc et al
rows.rationale: Detailed control allegations plausibly establish employee status, while identified underpayment weeks and substantial expenses support FLSA minimum-wage claims. Unauthorized deductions independently support IWPCA relief. Truth-in-Leasing allegations identify specific charges and escrow defects, although statutory miscitation and lease applicability create vulnerabilities. Missing exact weekly wage calculations could narrow claims but are unlikely to produce complete dismissal.

rows.case: Featherstone v. FCA US, LLC
Featherstone v. FCA US, LLC
Featherstone v. FCA US, LLC
rows.rationale: Specific workweeks, hours, rates, and earnings plausibly establish at least one FLSA overtime claim, particularly the February 2022 allegation of 40.7 hours paid entirely at straight time. These facts exceed conclusory pleading under Sixth Circuit standards. Regular-rate arithmetic and state-law theories invite challenges, but class-certification issues should not defeat all individual claims.

rows.case: Van Duser v. Tozzer Ltd.
Van Duser v. Tozzer Ltd.
Van Duser v. Tozzer Ltd.
rows.rationale: Specific pay rates, schedules, dated time-record alterations, unpaid training, and manager tip diversion plausibly support multiple wage claims. Missing tip-credit notice strongly supports NYLL minimum-wage liability. Shared scheduling, staffing, supplies, and direct supervision substantiate employer allegations. Wage-notice standing and payment-frequency remedies may be contested, but full dismissal is unlikely.

rows.case: Preston v. World Travel Holdings, Incorporated
Preston v. World Travel Holdings, Incorporated
Preston v. World Travel Holdings, Incorporated
rows.rationale: Specific unpaid tasks, daily time estimates, employer directives, and a dated paystub showing paid overtime plausibly establish uncompensated overtime under First Circuit pleading standards. Detailed bonus allegations provide another FLSA theory. Contract, unjust-enrichment, and nationwide-class issues may narrow the action but are unlikely to defeat every claim. No arbitration barrier appears in the complaint.

rows.case: Harrington v. Fb Hospitality, LLC
Harrington v. Fb Hospitality, LLC
Harrington v. Fb Hospitality, LLC
rows.rationale: Employment dates, cash wages, tip-pool allocations, and noncustomer-facing recipients plausibly establish minimum-wage violations through invalid tip credits. Federal and DC notice theories provide additional routes to survival. Joint-employer allegations and side-work theories face vulnerabilities, but those likely produce only partial dismissal. Overtime-specific pleading requirements are inapplicable, and no arbitration agreement appears.

rows.case: Cruz v. Jimenez Construction LLC
Cruz v. Jimenez Construction LLC
Cruz v. Jimenez Construction LLC
rows.rationale: Specific allegations of uncompensated loading and workday travel plausibly support D.C. wage claims independently of disputed Davis-Bacon entitlement. Employment dates, pay rates, and individual defendants’ control are detailed. Overtime allegations lack quantified weeks, and prevailing-wage theories face legal hurdles, but dismissal of every claim is unlikely. Contractor liability supplies an additional route against Mid-Atlantic.

rows.case: Owens v. Thompson
Owens v. Thompson
Owens v. Thompson
rows.rationale: Specific male comparators, salary figures, unequal experience credit, and alleged agency admissions plausibly support intentional sex-based pay discrimination under D.C. Circuit pleading standards. Detailed exhaustion dates and ongoing unequal pay support timeliness. Reliance on prior salary may invite defenses, and some remedies or historical promotion allegations may fail, but full dismissal appears unlikely.

rows.case: Covington v. Fmc & Associates, LLC
Covington v. Fmc & Associates, LLC
Covington v. Fmc & Associates, LLC
rows.rationale: Concrete allegations of 60–70-hour weeks, salary amounts, unpaid overtime, and nonexempt duties plausibly support wage claims. Named comparators, disparate work assignments, and discrimination complaints followed by termination support Section 1981 claims. DCHRA limitations and thin FLSA coverage allegations create vulnerabilities, but dismissal of every claim is unlikely.

rows.case: Cayton v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville & Davidson County
Cayton v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville & Davidson County
Cayton v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville & Davidson County
rows.rationale: The complaint plausibly alleges recurring overtime and a concrete policy withholding pay for hours 40–45, alongside hourly compensation inconsistent with the asserted exemption. Under Sixth Circuit pleading standards, missing example workweeks or pay rates likely is not fatal. Salary-basis and public-employer exceptions require factual development; collective-certification issues should not defeat the individual claim.
